question: What does core placement cost a wall-clock arm on the hybrid reference host, measured before the wall-clock lane was pinned?

provenance.host_description: 12th Gen Intel Core i9-12900F (8 P-cores / 16 threads at 5.0-5.1 GHz on CPUs 0-15, 8 E-cores at 3.8 GHz on CPUs 16-23, 24 logical CPUs, 30 MiB L3, Linux 6.8)
provenance.run_id: local: bare-metal reference host, interactive session

workload.design: three conditions interleaved P / unpinned / E within each round, 6 rounds

statistics.estimator: mean of the 6 per-round criterion means (ns)
statistics.method: percentile bootstrap over the 6 round means
statistics.limitation: Only the per-round summaries were retained from the session; the per-iteration criterion samples were not. This file therefore records summary statistics, not raw data, and cannot be re-bootstrapped at a different confidence or re-analysed per iteration. It is published as the resolvable source for the figures quoted in docs/BENCHMARKING.md rule 2 rather than as a re-analysable baseline; scripts/pin_exposure.py is what produces the re-analysable form.

derived.reading: The exposure ceiling. Larger than the 5.1/3.8 GHz clock ratio of 1.34 alone predicts; the residual is unmeasured, since no counter run separates frequency from per-cycle throughput on the E-cores.

Indistinguishable. On an idle host the scheduler kept the work on the P-cores, so the hazard did not fire in these 6 rounds. This is not evidence that it cannot fire: placement depends on what else the host is doing.

reading: The unpinned and P-core intervals overlap, so the defect was not firing on an idle host and no published figure is withdrawn on this evidence. The wall-clock arms are pinned regardless: the interval is blind to this failure mode, staying narrow when no migration happens and narrow and wrong when one does, and the pin costs nothing measurable because P-only is what the idle host already does.
